title: Capstone Part 1: Problem Framing and Data Foundation
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Capstone Part 1: Problem Framing and Data Foundation ##### Six weeks to build the wrong thing A data scientist joining a healthcare-logistics startup in Kochi was given her first real project: "predict which cold-chain shipments will spoil." She had good instincts. She pulled two years of IoT temperature logs, built features from rolling temperature excursions, trained a gradient-boosted classifier, tuned it with Optuna, and got 0.94 AUC. Six weeks of clean work. The review lasted eleven minutes. Operations asked when the prediction would arrive. "At delivery time, from the full temperature trace." Ops pointed out that at delivery time they already know whether the vial is spoiled — they have a thermometer. What they needed was a prediction at *dispatch*, from route, vehicle, ambient forecast, and box type, so they could swap to a better-insulated container before the truck left Kochi. Her model used the entire in-transit temperature curve. Every feature that made it 0.94 was unavailable at the moment a decision could be made. The model was not wrong; it answered a question nobody could act on. She rebuilt it. Dispatch-time features only, AUC 0.71 — and that model saved ₹1.2 crore in the first year, because a 0.71 model that fires when someone can still change the outcome beats a 0.94 model that fires when nobody can. **This is what Part 1 of your capstone is about.** Not modelling. The forty percent of the work that happens before you fit anything, and that determines whether the other sixty percent matters. ##### The gap between a business problem and an ML problem A business problem is a sentence someone says in a meeting. An ML problem is a specification with a target variable, a unit of prediction, a decision point, and a metric. Getting from one to the other is a translation, and translations lose information unless you are deliberate. ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Business problem
'We lose too much stock to spoilage'"] --> B["Decision
Which shipments get premium packaging?"] B --> C["Decision point
At dispatch, T-minus 2 hours"] C --> D["Prediction unit
One shipment"] D --> E["Target
spoiled = potency loss > 5% at delivery"] E --> F["Available features
ONLY what exists at T-2h"] F --> G["Metric
Recall at 15% flag budget"] G --> H["Baseline
Current rule: flag all monsoon routes"] H --> I["Success criterion
Beat baseline recall by 10pts
at the same flag budget"] ``` Walk that chain for your own capstone before writing a line of code. Each arrow is a place where a project quietly goes wrong. **The decision point is the load-bearing step.** Ask: *at what moment does someone do something differently because of this prediction?* Every feature must be observable strictly before that moment. This single discipline prevents the most expensive class of failure in applied ML. ##### Choosing a metric that reflects business value Accuracy is almost never the right metric, and Day 21 gave you the machinery. What Part 1 adds is the translation into money or user outcomes. Work through this: 1. **What are the four cells worth?** Write the cost of a false positive and a false negative in rupees or user-minutes. For the cold chain: a false positive means ₹340 of unnecessary premium packaging. A false negative means ₹18,000 of spoiled vaccine plus a stockout. That 53:1 ratio tells you immediately that recall dominates. 2. **What is the operating constraint?** Ops can upgrade packaging on at most 15% of shipments per day. So the metric is **recall at 15% flag rate**, not AUC. AUC averages over thresholds you will never use. 3. **Is it a ranking or a decision?** If a human reviews a queue, use precision@k or NDCG. If the system acts autonomously, use a thresholded metric at the operating point. 4. **Does calibration matter?** If downstream logic multiplies the probability by a cost, you need calibrated probabilities (Brier score, reliability curve), not just good ranking. Write this as a one-line **primary metric** plus two or three **guardrail metrics** that must not regress. Primary: recall@15%. Guardrails: precision ≥ 0.30, p95 inference latency < 200ms, no group's recall more than 10 points below the overall. ##### Scoping, success criteria, and baselines Your **project charter** is one page. It says: - **Problem** — one paragraph in business language. - **ML formulation** — task type, prediction unit, target definition, decision point. - **Data** — sources, period, expected volume, known gaps. - **Primary metric and guardrails** — with the operating point. - **Baseline** — what happens today, measured. - **Success criterion** — a number that decides ship/no-ship. - **Out of scope** — explicitly, so scope creep has something to bounce off. - **Risks** — leakage, label quality, distribution shift, fairness. **The baseline is not optional and it is not `DummyClassifier`.** Build three: | Baseline | What it tests | |---|---| | Trivial (majority class / global mean) | The floor. Sanity check that your metric is even sensible. | | Current process (the existing rule or human decision) | The bar you must clear to be worth deploying. | | Simple model (logistic regression, one-feature threshold) | Whether complexity is earning its keep. | If a logistic regression on five features gets 90% of the way there, the honest recommendation may be to ship it and stop. Sculley et al.'s *Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems* (2015) is largely a catalogue of what happens when teams skip this question — every model you deploy is a permanent maintenance liability, and a fancier one is a bigger liability. ##### A reproducible pipeline, not a notebook The deliverable for Part 1 is a repository, not a `.ipynb`. Use the cookiecutter-data-science layout or something close to it: ``` capstone-coldchain/ ├── README.md # charter + how to run ├── pyproject.toml # pinned deps ├── Makefile # make data / make features / make test ├── conf/ │ └── config.yaml # paths, params, seeds — no magic numbers in code ├── data/ │ ├── raw/ # immutable, gitignored, DVC-tracked │ ├── interim/ │ └── processed/ ├── src/ │ ├── ingest.py │ ├── clean.py │ ├── features.py │ ├── validate.py │ └── split.py ├── notebooks/ │ └── 01_eda.ipynb # exploration only; nothing production depends on it ├── reports/ │ ├── eda.md │ └── figures/ └── tests/ ├── test_clean.py └── test_features.py ``` The rule: **notebooks explore, modules produce.** Anything a downstream step depends on lives in `src/` and has a test. ```python # src/features.py from __future__ import annotations import pandas as pd DISPATCH_SAFE_COLUMNS = [ "route_id", "vehicle_type", "box_sku", "load_kg", "dispatch_hour_ist", "forecast_max_temp_c", "monsoon_flag", "origin_hub", "dest_district", "planned_transit_hours", ] def build_features(shipments: pd.DataFrame, routes: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame: """Dispatch-time features only. Anything observed in transit is banned.""" df = shipments.merge(routes, on="route_id", how="left", validate="many_to_one") df["dispatch_hour_ist"] = ( pd.to_datetime(df["dispatch_ts"], utc=True) .dt.tz_convert("Asia/Kolkata").dt.hour ) df["monsoon_flag"] = pd.to_datetime(df["dispatch_ts"]).dt.month.isin([6, 7, 8, 9]) df["load_ratio"] = df["load_kg"] / df["box_capacity_kg"] df["is_long_haul"] = df["planned_transit_hours"] > 18 # Historical route spoilage rate, computed with a strict time lag to avoid leakage. df = df.sort_values("dispatch_ts") df["route_hist_spoil_rate"] = ( df.groupby("route_id")["spoiled"] .transform(lambda s: s.shift(1).expanding().mean()) ) out = df[DISPATCH_SAFE_COLUMNS + ["route_hist_spoil_rate", "shipment_id", "spoiled"]] assert not out.columns.duplicated().any() return out ``` Two details worth copying. `validate="many_to_one"` on the merge turns a silent row explosion into a loud error. And the historical spoilage rate is computed with `.shift(1).expanding()` so a row never sees its own outcome — the most common leakage bug in tabular ML, and one that is invisible in cross-validation because the leak is present in both folds. ##### Leakage: the failure mode that looks like success Leakage is any information in your features that would not exist at prediction time. It produces beautiful validation scores and a model that collapses in production. The Kochi model was the extreme case; the subtle cases are worse because nobody catches them. The catalogue: - **Target leakage** — a feature that is a consequence of the target. `refund_issued` predicting `fraud`. `days_in_hospital` predicting `severe_case`. - **Temporal leakage** — using future data. Group statistics computed over the whole dataset, or a random split on time-series data. - **Train-test contamination** — fitting a scaler, imputer, or encoder on the full dataset before splitting. Always fit inside a `Pipeline` inside the CV loop; scikit-learn's *Common Pitfalls* page exists mostly for this. - **Duplicate rows across the split** — the same shipment logged twice lands in both train and test. - **Group leakage** — the same customer, patient, or device in both splits. Use `GroupKFold` keyed on the entity. The practical detector: **any feature with suspiciously high individual predictive power is guilty until proven innocent.** Fit a single-feature model on each column. If one gets 0.89 AUC alone, go find out why before you celebrate. ```python # src/split.py import pandas as pd def temporal_split(df: pd.DataFrame, ts_col: str, val_start: str, test_start: str): """Time-ordered split. Validation and test are strictly in the future.""" ts = pd.to_datetime(df[ts_col]) train = df[ts < val_start] val = df[(ts >= val_start) & (ts < test_start)] test = df[ts >= test_start] assert ts[train.index].max() < ts[val.index].min() assert ts[val.index].max() < ts[test.index].min() return train, val, test ``` Lock the test set away now. Touch it once, at the end of Part 2. Every peek costs you a little more of the guarantee it provides. ##### Data validation as code EDA tells you what the data looks like today. Validation tells you when it stops looking like that. Encode your EDA findings as assertions: ```python # src/validate.py import pandera as pa from pandera import Column, Check shipment_schema = pa.DataFrameSchema({ "shipment_id": Column(str, unique=True), "route_id": Column(str, Check.str_matches(r"^RT-\d{5}$")), "load_kg": Column(float, Check.in_range(0.5, 900.0)), "planned_transit_hours": Column(float, Check.in_range(0.5, 96.0)), "forecast_max_temp_c": Column(float, Check.in_range(-5.0, 52.0)), "dispatch_ts": Column("datetime64[ns, UTC]", nullable=False), "spoiled": Column(int, Check.isin([0, 1])), }, strict="filter", coerce=True) def validate_shipments(df): return shipment_schema.validate(df, lazy=True) # collect all errors, not just first ``` Every range in that schema came from an EDA finding. That is the point: EDA that ends in a notebook is a memory; EDA that ends in a schema is a guardrail that catches the day someone starts sending temperatures in Fahrenheit. ##### Rigorous EDA, briefly Your EDA report should answer, in writing: - **Shape and grain** — what does one row mean? Confirm uniqueness on the key. - **Target distribution** — class balance, and whether it drifts over time (plot monthly rate). - **Missingness** — per column, and *whether missingness itself is predictive*. A column missing 40% of the time only for one vendor is a signal and a red flag. - **Cardinality and rare categories** — 4,000 distinct route IDs with 3,200 appearing once needs a grouping strategy. - **Outliers** — real or instrument error? A 78°C reading is a broken sensor, not a hot truck. - **Time coverage** — gaps, regime changes, the week the logging system was rewritten. - **Leakage suspects** — the single-feature scan above. - **Group sizes** — for the fairness slices you committed to on Day 42. ##### Versioning the dataset Reproducibility means someone can regenerate your exact numbers. That needs three things pinned: code (git), environment (`pyproject.toml` with a lockfile), and data (DVC or an immutable, dated path in object storage). ```bash dvc add data/processed/features_v3.parquet git add data/processed/features_v3.parquet.dvc conf/config.yaml git commit -m "features v3: dispatch-safe only, adds route_hist_spoil_rate" dvc push ``` Record in the README: dataset version, row count, date range, git SHA of the generating code, and the config hash. Future-you, debugging a production discrepancy in November, will need exactly this. ##### Common mistakes - Starting with the model instead of the decision. - Using features unavailable at the decision point — the Kochi error. - Random-splitting time-ordered data. - Fitting preprocessing outside the CV loop. - No baseline, so "0.83 AUC" has no interpretation. - Choosing AUC when the business operates at one fixed threshold. - Defining the target loosely ("churned") without a precise window and condition. - Doing all the work in one notebook with cells run out of order. - Untracked data files, making results irreproducible next week. - Peeking at the test set during exploration. - Skipping the fairness slice-size check until it is too late to fix. ##### Hands-on: ship the charter first Your practical task is the charter plus the pipeline. Write the one-page charter *before* you write code — problem, ML formulation, success metric, baseline. Then build the pipeline that emits a cleaned, versioned, feature-engineered dataset. Time-box the charter to ninety minutes; its value is in forcing the decisions, not in polish. The mini project is the Part 1 artifact: a documented repo with framing, a tested ingest/clean/feature pipeline, a versioned dataset, an EDA report, and an established baseline plus evaluation plan. Two tests are the minimum bar — one asserting your feature function never emits a post-decision column, one asserting the temporal split has no overlap. Those two tests protect the whole capstone. The assignment asks you to defend your metric and baseline. Write it as if a sceptical VP is reading: what business value does this metric track, what does a one-point improvement mean in rupees or users, why this baseline, and specifically how your split and pipeline structure prevent leakage. If you cannot write that page, you are not ready for Part 2 — and finding that out now costs a day rather than six weeks. ##### Key takeaways - **Frame from the decision backwards**: decision → decision point → available features → target → metric. A great model at the wrong moment is worthless. - **Your metric must map to money or user outcomes**, evaluated at the operating point the business will actually use, with explicit guardrails. - **Always build three baselines** — trivial, current process, simple model — because "good" is only meaningful relative to what exists today. - **Leakage is the failure mode that looks like success.** Split by time and entity, fit preprocessing inside the pipeline, and interrogate any feature that is suspiciously predictive. - **Part 1's deliverable is a reproducible repository**, not a notebook: tested modules, a validated schema, a versioned dataset, and a written EDA report.
